newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Euro bourses fret over Wall St, elections, EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Euro bourses fret over Wall St, elections, EMU.

text.p: European bourses fell on Tuesday even before Wall Street opened lower as London suffered pre-election jitters and continental markets fretted over European monetary union.

The dollar continued slipping against the yen and mark following comments from a senior Bundesbanker that EMU (economic and monetary union) should be delayed if Germany could not meet the entry criteria.

Frankfurt fell 1.78 percent as a result but share markets across the continent also worried about the health of the U.S. market, with Wall Street guru Warren Buffett saying most stocks were overvalued.

The mood was further depressed by the ever-present fear that the U.S. central bank would make a preemptive strike against inflation by raising interest rates when its Federal Open Market Committee meets on March 25.
Wall Street did little to help by opening lower, although the Dow Jones Industrial Average later recovered a little and slipped in and out of profit.
Investors in Europe, where markets tumbled on Monday, also had worries of their own.

London, which shrugged off Prime Minister John Major's announcement of a May 1 parliamentary election on Monday, started worrying about a six-week campaign and the prospect of a change in government. By mid afternoon the FTSE-100 index was down 19.0 points at 4,354.3.
The election date came as no surprise to markets, but with the opposition far ahead in opinion polls, traders began to contemplate life under a Labour government.
Financial markets are traditionally hostile to Labour, but leader Tony Blair has dragged the party towards the centre and made efforts to woo the business community.
"Even though everybody expects Labour to win, the election campaign will still be a factor, it's another reason for people to sit on their hands and stay out of the market," one trader said.

Speculation centres on what tax plans Labour will reveal if it wins. "It is not a happy scenario. There is support from the weight of money argument but I would not want to be active buyer here," the trader said.
Other European equity markets were likewise weak. In Paris the CAC-40 index was 11.3 points or 0.44 percent lower at 2,577.08 after tumbling two percent on Monday.
But Germany suffered the most with the DAX closing down 59.8 points at 3,291.19.

Concern is growing that Bonn might fail to cut its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product this year, a target for EMU membership, forcing a delay in the project's scheduled start in January 1999.

Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher was quoted on Tuesday as doubting that Germany could meet convergency targets and the start of EMU could have to be delayed. "If Germany can't meet EMU targets the markets are going to fall sharply," one senior trader said.
Frankfurt also buzzed about Hoesch-Krupp's plan to bid for steel giant Thyssen AG. Shares in both were suspended by the German stock exchange.
Thyssen has said it would use "all appropriate measures" to ward off its smaller rival.
On foreign exchange markets, the dollar slipped to 1.6824 marks from 1.6901 in European trading late on Monday, and to 122.80 yen from 123.63.
As on the equity markets, Kuehbacher's comments on EMU and U.S. interest rates were major talking points. Dealers said Kuehbacher had only heightened confusion over EMU.

"Kuehbacher's comments are surprisingly forthright, but the Buba guys can say what they like -- it's still down to the politicians to make the decision," said Thomas Rayner, economist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull.
Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony to the Joint Economic Committee on Thursday will be watched closely for clues on U.S. monetary policy.
"Greenspan has seemed to indicate that he would prefer some pre-emptive tightening, it's a very close call but the market risk is that he won't raise rates," said a German bank dealer.

Announcement of a Japanese government scheme to improve land sales helped the yen, along with comments from a Bank of Japan official which dealers interpreted as a check on falling long-term interest rates.
CURRENCIES AT 1500 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 1.6824 marks and 122.80 yen, compared with Monday's late European levels of 1.6901 marks and 123.63 yen.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1500 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was down 19.0 points at 4,354.3.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was down 11.3 points at 2,577.08.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index closed down 59.80 (1.78 percent) at 3,291.19. In later electronic trading, the IBIS index was down 24.48 percent at 3,312.63.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed at $346.30 an ounce in the afternoon after a morning fixing at $347.40 and compared with $350.25 at the close on Monday. Silver was at $5.18, compared with $5.23 on Monday.
